name: Golestandt

facts.text: Level 80, 300,000 health. Takes no damage outside her lair; breathes fire at every tenth of her health (90% down to 10%); her Dragon's Breath halves Heat resist; she glares, stuns and roars across the land.
Granite giant stonelords, pounders and outlookers come to her: at most six in a fight, at 85/70/55/40/25/10% health.
Her waking roar: 'I will grind your bones and shred your flesh!'. Her taunts single out the class of the raider she kills.

Gender: the script's emotes say 'his', but they are a template shared word for word with Cuuldurach's script. Albion bot chat, period player talk calling Cuuldurach 'the only male dragon', and the lore bible's other dragons make her female; this entry says she.
Period sizes: 125-160 (Feb 2003), down to 17-24 over two to three hours by August 2003.
Dartmoor's granite giants drop Ancient Granite Stones, turned in for experience to an NPC upstairs at the back of the inn (named Eugen Aldar in a 2010 comment).

June 2002: about 350 gathered for a dragon hunt and the zone crashed before she appeared; later that month 150-200 were wiped in about twenty minutes by fire of about 5,000; in July a kill in about ten minutes was reported.
Her script picks one player to stare at and 'prepares a massive attack', looks mindfully around, and has a roaming glare and a stun; dragonscales drop from the dragons (LootGeneratorDragonscales).
Lucius Valerius, Hywel of Caerwent, Marcus Fabricius, Sir Pellam, Sir Bedwyr Alder, the Bed and the folk etymologies of her name are Living Server writing.

story:
Golestandt is the stone dragon of Dartmoor, as old as the moor, and she sleeps in a warm granite hollow at its southern end that the Cornish drovers call the Bed. She and the Bed are one stone: outside her lair nothing harms her, because the granite takes every blow for her. The granite giants that lie in the heather are her get, shards of the Bed that walked away; outlookers, pounders and stonelords come to her as she bleeds, one for each sixth of her strength, and Moran the Mighty keeps the high ground east of her, her guard or her rival depending on who tells it.

Albion learned her name once, in Uther's day, when the Roman landholder Lucius Valerius vanished from his house and Sir Arward's thirty knights rode south after him. Only their scribe Hywel's scorched journal came home, falling out of a clear sky onto Prydwen Keep with one word branded on its last page. Generations earlier the Roman armourer Marcus Fabricius had forged heat-wards that held against her once; ever since, her fire eats the ward first and the man second, and she breathes once for every tenth of her strength lost, so the second breath always lands harder.

When the dragons woke, three hundred and fifty of Albion gathered on Dartmoor and she did not deign to rise; a few weeks later she broke a muster of two hundred in twenty minutes. Later that summer a raid that fought her only in the Bed and braced before each tenth brought her down, and Albion has grown better at her since. She knows men by their trades and taunts each by his calling, fixes on one raider for a crushing blow, and stuns those her wandering glare finds. Her lair keeps scales, a dulled Roman helmet and a knight's spur, not gold. Some frontier riders say the drake of the Pennines, Draco Magnificens, is her heir. The Church fears the moor is spreading north. Albion goes south to put her back to sleep.
legend: When the dragons first woke, the whole realm stood on Dartmoor to look at her, and she would not come out. Never say her name inside the moor; old raid leaders swear she listens. The rules are old and they work. Fight her in the Bed and nowhere else, because outside it she takes nothing. Stack heat resist twice, because her first breath eats the ward and the second eats you. She breathes at every tenth of her health: heal up and brace before each one, nine times a fight. Keep a party on the granite giants, who come one per sixth of her health, six at most. Heal whoever she stares at; she is about to hit him very hard. Watch her eyes, not her mouth: her glare stuns. In the summer she first woke it took two hundred and failed; now twenty-four who know her can do it, slowly. And leave the table in the house of Lucius alone on the way south.

loremasterTopic.text: The stone dragon of Dartmoor, as old as the moor. Outside her lair nothing harms her; inside it she answers every tenth part of her strength with fire, and her breath eats the heat-ward off your armour. Fight her in her lair.

bookPage: Fifth day. The ground lurched under us at noon and every horse screamed. A voice came out of the south that was not a voice so much as weather, and it said that it would grind our bones. Sir Arward laughed and drew his sword. I am writing this on my knee. The giants are standing up all around us now, dozens of them, and they are not looking at us. They are looking south, as dogs look at a door when their mistress comes home. I have written the names and trades of all thirty of us on the first page. I do not know why I feel I should not have.

chapters.title: The Bed of Granite
chapters.text:
The old Britons of the west called Dartmoor the giants' floor. The tors, they said, were stones the giants had left lying when they went away, and a careful shepherd did not sleep in their shadow. They had half of it. The granite giants never went away; they lie in the heather with the turf grown over their backs and stand up when nobody is watching. What the Britons did not say aloud is what the giants lie down around.

At the southern end of the moor, past the last ruined farm, the granite falls into a hollow that the Cornish drovers call the Bed. It is the only place on Dartmoor where the heather will not grow. The stone there is warm in winter. Sheep that stray into it come out with their fleeces singed in a pattern like the grain of the rock, and the drovers sell such sheep cheap, because nobody wants to eat them.

The Bed is Golestandt's lair, and it is older than the name of any king. The Camelot loremasters place it in the age of the first stones, before the Keltoi raised their circles on Salisbury Plain, and some of them argue that the circles were raised in imitation of the tors around her: a ring of granite set to watch a sleeper.

The Bed explains the first rule every raid learns. Outside her lair, nothing harms her. The drovers' version is that the moor is her armour, and that away from her bed every blow struck at her is taken by the granite instead, the way a tor takes a lightning stroke and does not notice. The Inconnu, who have their own reasons to study things that do not die, say it more precisely: she and the Bed are one stone, and a stone can only be broken where it lies. Either way the lesson is the same. Lure her out onto the open moor and you are fighting Dartmoor itself, and Dartmoor has never lost a fight.

chapters.title: The Name in the Journal
chapters.text:
Albion learned her name exactly once, and paid thirty knights for it.

In Uther's day a Roman, Lucius Valerius, kept a house two days south of the Cornish road, on the last good ground before the moor turns to bog. He was the last of the old province's landholders in the west, and stubborn about it. One autumn his letters to Camelot stopped. Uther sent Sir Arward with thirty knights and a scribe, Hywel of Caerwent, whose task was to write everything down.

Hywel's journal survives in pieces at Prydwen Keep. The house of Lucius, he wrote, stood empty, the table laid for a meal and the meal eaten, the doors barred from inside. On the third day the boulders began to move: Sir Pellam rode after one that stood up and walked from the fire, and came back at dawn and would not say where he had been. On the fifth day the ground lurched at noon and a voice came out of the south that Hywel called more weather than voice, promising to grind their bones. Arward laughed and drew his sword. The giants were standing all around them by then, dozens, and Hywel noted that they were not looking at the knights. They were looking south.

The rest is burnt. The journal fell out of a clear sky onto the walk of Prydwen Keep that winter, scorched through, and on the last page one word was pressed into the vellum as if with a hot iron, in a hand that was not Hywel's.

What the word means is argued to this day. The Cornish drovers say Golestandt is old west-country for 'the stone that stands', and that the knights merely wrote down what the giants called her. The scholars of Camelot answer that it belongs to no tongue they know. The Inconnu, asked, said only that it is the name she gave Hywel, and that she gave it so that someone would carry it home. The house of Lucius still stands. Its table is still laid.

chapters.title: The Stone Mother
chapters.text:
Albion's minstrels have sung her as the stone mother of Dartmoor for as long as anyone has sung her at all, and the raid leaders who have heard her taunt them sometimes call her he; the argument is older than any guild. The minstrels have the better case. The granite giants are hers.

They are not her servants in the way the drakoran serve Xanxicar. They are more like her get: shards of the Bed that walked away, the drovers say, and grew. They have their own orders. The outlookers stand on the tors and watch the roads; the pounders do the moor's heavy work, breaking the stone a giant needs to mend itself; the stonelords command the rest and are the only giants who will stand in the Bed itself. When raiders come into her lair she does not call all of them at once. She calls them as she bleeds, one more each time another sixth of her strength runs out into the granite, no more than six in a fight, as a mother calls her children one by one from the fields. A raid that leaves no party to meet them learns why.

Every giant carries a stone in its chest, heavy and grey, which raiders call Ancient Granite Stones. A man named Eugen Aldar buys them, upstairs at the back of the inn on the Cornish road, and will pay good experience for them to anyone seasoned enough; he says he is building a wall, and nobody has seen the wall.

Moran the Mighty is not her get. He stands on the high ground east of the Bed, taller than the tors, and the wind on his hill does what he says. The drovers say he is her guard and watches the roads she cannot. The frontier riders say he is her rival, a giant of the air who has been waiting a thousand years for the stone to crack. Moran has never said, and nobody who has stood on his hill long enough to ask him has stayed on it.

chapters.title: The Ward-Eater
chapters.text:
Lucius Valerius did not live two days from the Bed by accident. His grandfather had been a legate of the old province, sent west with a cohort and an armourer called Marcus Fabricius to put the moor under Rome's law, and the family had stayed to finish the work.

Fabricius was a maker of wards. The Romans had learned in the east to forge a ward against fire into a breastplate, a heat-ward, so that a soldier could walk through a burning town. When the cohort first marched south across the moor and the Bed woke, Fabricius's wards held. Forty legionaries stood in her fire and came out blackened and alive, and the legate wrote to Rome that the beast of the moor had been mastered. It was the only time anyone has written that.

She learned. The second time the cohort came south, her first breath did not burn the men. It burned the wards. Fabricius's own account, copied by a Camelot clerk from a tablet found in the house of Lucius, says that the breastplates glowed and dulled and the soldiers felt the protection go out of them like warmth out of a hearth; and that her second breath, a little while later, killed thirty of the forty. Since that day her fire has eaten the ward first and the man second. Every Albion raid that faces her stacks its heat-wards twice and still feels the second breath land harder than the first.

Fabricius also recorded the rhythm the raids still fight to. She breathed, he wrote, not when she pleased but when she was wounded past a mark, once for every tenth part of her strength that ran out, as a smith quenches a blade in stages; and between the marks she did not breathe at all. The legate's men learned to heal and ward between the marks and to brace before each. So do Albion's healers, nine times a fight, from the first tenth to the last.

chapters.title: The Summer of the Gathering
chapters.text:
For centuries after Arward nobody went south on Dartmoor on purpose. The realm knew the name and the burnt smear and the stories, and left the Bed alone. Then the dragons of all three realms woke within a season of each other, and Albion went to look.

The Camelot Herald calls it the summer of the gathering. The companies of half the realm rode for Dartmoor at once, three hundred and fifty at the count of Marshal Gareth of Prydwen Keep, and stood in the heather around the Bed waiting for her to show herself. The moor buckled under them; the drovers swear the tors leaned. She did not come. For two hours she lay under the granite and let them wait, and then they rode home, and the minstrels have made a song of it ever since: the day Albion came to Dartmoor and the dragon was not at home.

She was at home a few weeks later, when a muster of nearly two hundred went south under a knight of Castle Sauvage named Sir Bedwyr Alder. That company found her awake and broke in the time it takes to say a long mass. The survivors measured her fire by what was left of their priests, and the figure they brought back to Camelot became a proverb in the guildhalls: five thousand a breath, and the second worse.

The first company to bring her down did it before that summer was out, according to the roll kept at Prydwen Keep, by fighting her in the Bed and nowhere else and by bracing before each tenth as Fabricius had written. The roll does not say whose company it was; three guilds of Camelot claim it, and the Herald, wisely, has never chosen. What the roll does record is the change that followed. Prydwen Keep stopped sending crowds south and began sending veterans, companies of a few dozen who had stood in the Bed before, with priests chosen for steady hands rather than loud prayers. They take hours over it now, and they come home. She has not grown kinder. Albion has grown better at her.

chapters.title: Every Trade Its Taunt
chapters.text:
She knows men by their trades. Every raider who has died in the Bed has heard her name his calling as he fell: foolish knight, foolish wizard, foolish friar, his flesh a splendid meal; or, to a minstrel who once tried to sing her a verse, that Albion's dark ages would end sooner if his kind were weeded out. She called one cleric crunchy. The cleric's guild still sells badges of it.

Where she learned the trades is part of Arward's story. Hywel the scribe listed the thirty in his first entry, each by name and calling: armsmen, a paladin, two friars, a mercenary from the Black Mountains, a scout. The Inconnu believe she took Hywel's list along with the rest of his journal and learned it, and that every raid since has been sorted against it. The Camelot loremasters prefer a simpler account: she has watched men cross her moor for a thousand years, and she pays attention.

The trades matter in the fight. When she settles on one raider and stares at him, she is choosing, and a moment later she gathers a massive blow for that one alone; the raid that does not heal the chosen loses him. When she rests between breaths she looks mindfully round the Bed, and her glare wanders until it fixes on someone else. Those who meet it are stunned where they stand. Old Albion raid leaders tell their healers to watch her eyes, not her mouth, because the mouth only tells you a tenth has passed. The eyes tell you who she wants.

Her waking roar is the one thing she says to everyone at once. It comes across the whole of Dartmoor when she takes to the sky, the same words Hywel wrote down in Uther's day, and every drover between the Cornish road and the Labyrinth's mouth knows them: I will grind your bones and shred your flesh.

chapters.title: What the Bed Keeps
chapters.text:
She does not hoard gold. The raids that have stood in the Bed after a kill report the same few things, and the accounts agree on them more closely than on anything else about her.

There are scales, shed over the centuries and grown into the granite like mica, and Albion's armourers prize them above any metal; a dragonscale worked into a shield remembers the fire and turns it. There is the burnt smear that runs north out of the Bed toward the ruined farms, which the drovers say is the track of her first waking and which no grass has crossed since. There are the dead, or what she left of them: a Roman helmet with a heat-ward gone dull, which Prydwen Keep claims was Fabricius's own, and a knight's spur that the descendants of Sir Pellam say was his. Nobody has found Lucius Valerius. His table in the house to the north is still laid, and the raids that pass it on the way south have made a custom of leaving it alone.

There is one more thing the Bed may keep, and here the accounts divide. In the Pennine Mountains, on the old frontier, the riders of Castle Sauvage tell of a younger dragon that hunts the high passes, a great drake they call Draco Magnificens. The frontier riders say he is hers: a shard of the Bed that took wing instead of walking, as the giants walked. The Camelot loremasters answer that a dragon of the Pennines has nothing to do with a dragon of Dartmoor, that the drake has no granite in him, and that the riders want a grander story than a frontier beast. The drovers of the Cornish road settle it their own way. They say that on the nights the drake flies south, she wakes.

chapters.title: If the Stone Stands Up
chapters.text:
What she wants is the one question nobody in Albion can answer from her own words, because she does not explain herself. The answers come from those who watch her.

The drovers say she wants to be left in her Bed, and that every waking is only a sleeper turning over to swat a fly. They point to the summer of the gathering, when three hundred and fifty stood around her lair and she did not bother to rise. The Church of Camelot says she wants the moor to spread. Its priests in Cornwall keep a record of the heather line on the north edge of Dartmoor, and they claim it has moved a mile toward the Cornish road since Uther's day, and that the granite giants have been seen standing in fields that were farms when Lucius Valerius kept his house. The Inconnu, who rarely volunteer anything, said once that she wants what all the old powers want, which is for the age of men to end so that the world can go back to sleep.

Her taunts lean toward the Inconnu. She tells Albion's champions that their dark ages would end if their kind were weeded out, and she says it as though it were a kindness.

If she ever stood up and walked north, the loremasters agree on the order of it: the giants first, out of the heather, all of them; Moran's wind on the high road; then the Bed itself, the stone that stands. Cornwall would go in a season. The barrows under the stones on Salisbury Plain would wake, because the old dead answer the old powers. Camelot has walls and has never tested them against a moor.

So Albion goes south. A raid in the Bed is not glory, the old raid leaders say, whatever the Herald writes. It is the realm putting a sleeper back to sleep, and doing it again whenever she wakes.
